passages.happening:
“One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour” (verse 1). A man lame from birth is being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he is put every day to beg. He asks Peter and John for money.

Peter looks straight at him. “Look at us,” he says. The man looks up, expecting a gift. “But Peter said, ‘Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk’” (verse 6).

Peter takes him by the right hand and helps him up, and at once his feet and ankles are made strong. He jumps up and walks, and goes into the temple courts with them, “walking and leaping and praising God” (verse 8). Everyone recognizes him as the man who used to sit begging at the gate, and they are filled with wonder.
passages.hearers:
The ninth hour was about three in the afternoon. Day hours were counted from sunrise. At that time the second daily sacrifice was offered in the temple, as Josephus tells, and many people came to pray. Peter and John still keep the hours of prayer their people kept. Following Jesus has not made them leave the temple.

No one knows for sure which gate was called ‘Beautiful’; no other ancient writer uses that name. Many think it was the Nicanor Gate, a great gate of bronze on the east side of the temple, leading into the inner courts. Others suggest other gates. Either way, it was a busy entrance where worshippers passed.

Giving to the poor was a large part of Jewish devotion, and people on the way to prayer were likely to give. So beggars sat where worshippers walked by. This man had been carried there every day. He was more than forty years old (4:22), lame since birth. He had lived his whole life at the edge of the place of worship, looking in.

Peter has no money. What he gives is better than what the man asked for. And notice what Luke says next: the man goes into the temple courts. He has sat at the gate for years. Now he goes in, on his own feet, praising God.
passages.ot: The prophets had promised that when God came to save his people, the lame would be healed. “Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy” (Isaiah 35:6). Luke's words, ‘walking and leaping’, sound like Isaiah's. For those who knew the prophets, this was a sign that the time of God's salvation had come.
passages.hard:
The man was healed at once. Many who are sick or disabled today pray for healing that does not come. What does this story say to them?

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. This man did not show any faith before he was healed; he was hoping for coins. Paul begged the Lord three times to take away his ‘thorn in the flesh’ and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He left his friend Trophimus “sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). None of these men are blamed. Seeking a doctor is not a failure of faith either; Paul called his friend Luke “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14).

Christians differ on how God heals today. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians expect God to heal often in answer to prayer and through gifts of healing, and some teach that healing is promised to believers now through Christ's death, pointing to Isaiah 53:4 and Matthew 8:17. Many others believe that God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills, but that the apostles' signs of healing belonged in a special way to the founding of the church, and that full healing waits for the resurrection, when God “will wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4). All of them pray for the sick, as James tells the church to do (James 5:14-15).

And if you live with a disability or an illness that has not been healed, this story is not a judgment on your faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The man asked for a little and was given much more. Ask what you are asking God for, and whether you are ready to receive something other than you expected. And notice Peter's honesty: he did not pretend to have what he did not have. He gave what he had, which was Jesus.

passages.t: Not our power: the name of Jesus
passages.happening:
The healed man clings to Peter and John, and the people come running to them in Solomon's Colonnade, amazed.

Peter speaks. “Men of Israel, why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?” (verse 12). The God of their fathers has glorified his servant Jesus. “You handed Him over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though he had decided to release Him” (verse 13). They asked for a murderer to be released instead. “You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of the fact” (verse 15).

It is Jesus' name, he says, and the faith that comes through him, that has made this man strong, “in your presence” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Solomon's Colonnade was a long covered walkway along the east side of the temple's outer court, its roof held up by rows of columns. People gathered and talked there. Jesus had walked and taught there (John 10:23), and the believers would meet there (5:12).

Peter at once turns the attention away from himself and John. They are not holy men with special power. The power belongs to Jesus.

He gives Jesus a string of titles. God's ‘servant’. ‘The Holy and Righteous One’. ‘The Author of life’: the Greek word means the founder, the one who leads the way and begins something. The crowd asked for Barabbas, a man who took life (Luke 23:19). They gave up the one who gives life. Peter wants them to feel the irony.

‘The name’ in the Bible stands for the person himself, with all his authority. To act ‘in the name of Jesus’ is not to use a magic word. It is to act by his authority and depend on him.
passages.ot:
‘The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’ is how God named himself to Moses at the burning bush: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). Peter is saying that the God of Israel, their own God, is the one who has acted.

‘His servant’ and ‘glorified’ echo Isaiah's servant of the Lord: “Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13). That servant suffers before he is lifted up. ‘The Righteous One’ comes from the same song: “My righteous Servant will justify many” (Isaiah 53:11).
passages.hard: ‘You handed Him over’ and ‘You killed the Author of life’. As at 2:23, these are the words of a Jew to his own people in Jerusalem, weeks after the event, and in the next breath he says, ‘I know that you acted in ignorance’ (verse 17), and offers them blessing. They are a call to turn, not a charge against the Jewish people. The note on 2:22-28 sets out how such verses were misused against Jews for centuries, and why this site rejects that reading.
passages.asks: Peter could have let the crowd admire him. He pointed them to Jesus instead. Ask whom people end up admiring when God does something good through you. And ask whether you know Jesus' name as a word you say, or as a person you depend on.

passages.t: You acted in ignorance: turn back
passages.happening:
“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders” (verse 17). God has fulfilled what all the prophets foretold, that his Christ would suffer.

“Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away, that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that He may send Jesus, the Christ, who has been appointed for you” (verses 19-20). Heaven must receive Jesus, Peter says, “until the time comes for the restoration of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Peter calls them ‘brothers’. He has just told them they rejected the Messiah, and now he speaks as one of them. Acting ‘in ignorance’ does not mean they did nothing wrong. It means they did not know who Jesus was. Jesus himself had prayed from the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Peter's sermon is that prayer being answered.

‘Wiped away’ means wiped out, as writing is wiped off a page. Sins are not just covered over. They are erased.

‘Times of refreshing’ and ‘the restoration of all things’ look ahead to the day when Jesus returns and God puts the whole world right. Until then, Peter says, Jesus is in heaven. The present time is the time to turn.
passages.ot:
The prophets often call Israel to ‘return’ or ‘turn back’ to God, with the promise that God will forgive. Isaiah: “I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more” (Isaiah 43:25).

‘The restoration of all things’ gathers up the prophets' hope of a renewed world, such as Isaiah's promise of “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17).
passages.hard:
Does ‘the restoration of all things’ (verse 21) mean that everyone will finally be saved? The Greek word is apokatastasis. Some Christians in the early centuries, Origen among them in the 200s, used it for the hope that all would at last be restored to God, and some Christians hold a form of that hope today.

Most Christian traditions have not read this verse that way. In context Peter speaks of what God promised through the prophets, a renewal of the world that also includes judgment. Two verses later he warns that whoever will not listen to the prophet like Moses “will be completely cut off from among his people” (verse 23). So most take the restoration of all things to mean the renewal of creation and the setting right of God's people, not the certain salvation of every person. The passage holds out hope and urgency together.
passages.asks: Peter treats his hearers as people who did not know, and who can now know and turn. Ask whether you treat people who reject Jesus as enemies to beat, or as brothers and sisters who have not yet seen. And ask whether there is anything you need to have wiped away. The offer is open.

passages.t: The prophet like Moses, and Abraham's blessing
passages.happening:
Peter reminds them of Moses' words: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you” (verse 22). Everyone who does not listen will be cut off. All the prophets from Samuel on, he says, spoke of these days.

“And you are sons of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your fathers when He said to Abraham, ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed’” (verse 25).

“When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Many Jews in the first century looked for ‘the prophet’ Moses had promised, a figure who would speak God's words like Moses did. In John's Gospel people ask John the Baptist, ‘Are you the Prophet?’ (John 1:21). Peter says that prophet has come, and it is Jesus.

Peter tells his hearers who they are: heirs of the prophets and of God's covenant with Abraham. He is not talking to outsiders. He is talking to the family to whom the promises were made.

And he ends with blessing. God sent his servant ‘first to you’. ‘First’ hints that others will come after: the families of the earth. But the order matters. The good news came to Israel first, and it came as blessing.
passages.ot:
The words about the prophet like Moses come from Deuteronomy 18:15-19: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Peter joins to it a warning in the language of the Law about being cut off from the people.

The promise to Abraham is from Genesis: “And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice” (Genesis 22:18; compare Genesis 12:3). Peter reads ‘your offspring’ as pointing to Jesus, Abraham's descendant, through whom the blessing comes.
passages.asks: The sermon that began with a lame man ends with a whole people invited to be blessed. Ask whether you hear the gospel as a threat or as a blessing, and how others hear it from you. Peter's last word was not ‘or else’ but ‘to bless you’.
